To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) visual representations that are learned from egocentric images can be made more invariant to ego-motion by using proprioceptive motor information to regularize the feature learning process; b) this regularization can improve the performance of the resulting representations for a variety of visual recognition tasks.

we propose an unsupervised learning framework to learn visual representations that are equivariant to ego-motions, and that we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in three datasets and show that features learned in an unsupervised manner from video captured on a driving platform significantly improve large-scale scene classification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of how to learn image representations that are invariant to the ego-motion.
how to exploit the rich source of information provided by the motor system to improve visual learning and representation.
the development of a visual system that learns from video in a manner that is grounded in the physics of the sensor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method learns image representations that are invariant to the camera pose, but are sensitive to the ego-motion.

our work demonstrates that the use of proprioceptive information in the form of motor commands can improve the quality of visual representations learned from egocentric videos, which can in turn be used in a variety of visual tasks.
we propose to exploit proprioception to learn visual representations that are robust to ego-motion and thus improve visual recognition and scene prediction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how to learn visual representations that are invariant to the camera motion.
we learn a visual representation of the scene that is invariant to the camera ego-motion.
we learn visual features from egocentric videos by exploiting their proprioceptive signals, and the features are equivariant to ego-motions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the physical source of visual data should be considered when training visual models.
learning image representations that are equivariant to ego-motions can significantly boost performance of visual learning systems.
learning image representations that are equivariant to ego-motions is an effective and general approach for unsupervised feature discovery.
